scenario: AITA for being home all day and refusing to cook for my mom? | I'm a female in my senior year of high school and I have a younger sister in grade 10. As most of you know, schools have been closed for a while now and won't reopen for at least another month. My dad gets to work from home, but my mom still has to go out to her office. My school just started online teaching, and we've been getting a lot of assignments to complete. However, my mom expects us to make dinner basically every night because "we're home all day". That really annoyed me because yeah "we're home all day" but we have school work to do. I got upset and asked her why doesn't she cook, since she always finishes work at 5 pm and her office is like 6 minutes from home. Well, once she got home today and saw there was no dinner prepared, she got pissed and started screaming at me how she's so ashamed of us and how we're useless. When I explained how yes we're home all day but doesn't mean we have the whole day off, she got even more mad and said that it doesn't take that long to cook. I refuted by "why don't you cook then?" For more context, my mom is an awful cook. She literally puts no effort into learning or looking up recipes. My dad is an excellent cook. He's tried to teach her before, but she refuses to learn and complains. Before, he would cook for us almost every day, even if he came home late from work (he has a high demanding job so his hours range but he's home 6 pm the EARLIEST, sometimes as late as 9 or even 10 pm. + 30-40 minutes one way commuting). And what does he come home to? Either a low effort flavourless meal from my mom, or my mom sitting on her ass watching TV and asking him what's he's gonna make for dinner. So my dad is forced to make dinner at a late hour so he can eat. More recently, he would just eat fast-food before coming home because he doesn't expect dinner to be on the table. However, he asks if us girls are hungry and offers to cook something for us to eat because he's worried that our mom didn't make us a proper meal. I'm a good cook too (self taught), and I try to help out if I don't have too much homework to do. I did a lot of the cooking during the first 3 weeks before online school started, as well as baking lots of treats like breads, cookies, meringues etc. Also, my dad does practically all the chores in the house, while my mom spends all her time sitting on her ass watching TV. So AITA for not cooking dinner today and telling my mom to not expect dinner every time she comes home? Also, my dad ended cooking in the end today.

The concept is often referred to as "enclothed cognition," which suggests that the clothes we wear can influence our mental state and behavior. When you wear a suit and tie, you may feel more put together, professional, and prepared to take on challenges. The formal attire can signal to your brain that you're in a more serious and important mode, which can boost your confidence and self-assurance. Additionally, wearing a suit and tie can also affect how others perceive you. People may view you as more competent, trustworthy, and authoritative when you're dressed in formal attire. This can lead to a positive feedback loop, where you feel more confident because you're receiving positive cues from others. It's also worth noting that the psychological impact of wearing a suit and tie can be highly personal and subjective. Some people may feel restricted or uncomfortable in formal attire, while others may feel empowered and confident. Ultimately, it's essential to wear what makes you feel good about yourself and helps you project the image you want to convey. So, if wearing a suit and tie makes you feel confident, that's great! Own it and rock that confidence. Do you have a particular occasion or event where you feel like your suit and tie give you an extra boost of confidence?
